content: Resin-based composite (RBC) is widely recognized as a suitable material for restoring carious lesions in posterior permanent teeth that require surgical intervention. Despite its thermal conductivity being similar to that of natural tooth structure, postoperative hypersensitivity remains a concern in some cases. Historically, dental cavity liners have been employed to shield the dental pulp from the potentially toxic effects of certain restorative materials and to mitigate thermal sensitivity by creating an insulating barrier between the restorative material and the remaining tooth structure. This review is an update of a Cochrane Review initially published in 2016. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the effects of using dental cavity liners in Class I and Class II resin-based composite restorations for posterior permanent teeth in both children and adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, including Cochrane Oral Health's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS, up to November 12, 2018. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date during the search process. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the use of cavity liners under Class I and Class II posterior resin-based composite restorations in permanent teeth. Both parallel and split-mouth study designs were considered. Standard Cochrane methodologies were employed for data collection and analysis. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, assessed study eligibility, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. When necessary, study authors were contacted for clarification. A total of eight studies, involving over 700 participants, were included in the review. These studies compared the use of dental cavity liners to no liners in Class I and Class II resin-based composite restorations. Seven of the studies assessed postoperative hypersensitivity using various methods. The evidence regarding postoperative hypersensitivity was inconsistent, with some studies showing a benefit at certain time points, while others did not. The overall quality of evidence was deemed low, and all included studies were judged to have either unclear or high risk of bias. Four trials investigated the longevity of restorations. Two of these studies were classified as having a high risk of bias, while the other two had an unclear risk of bias. At a one-year follow-up, no significant differences in restoration failure rates were observed between groups. Three of the four studies reported no failures in either group, while the fourth study reported a risk ratio (RR) of 1.00 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.07 to 15.00). Similarly, at a two-year follow-up, no failures were reported in either group. The quality of evidence for restoration longevity was also considered low. Furthermore, no adverse events were reported in any of the included studies. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the impact of dental cavity liners on postoperative hypersensitivity in Class I and Class II resin-based composite restorations for permanent posterior teeth is inconsistent and of low quality. Additionally, there is no evidence to suggest a difference in the longevity of restorations placed with or without cavity liners.
